Harpreet had run to the canal and back every morning for five weeks, training for the district athletics trials. Then her cousin's wedding kept the whole house awake till three, and she slept through the morning run. When she woke, the sun was already over the fields.
"That's it," she told her cousin Sukhi flatly. "I've ruined it. Five weeks for nothing." She put her running shoes in the trunk under the bed. For three days she didn't go out, not even for a short walk.
"You missed one day," Sukhi said. "One. Not five weeks."
"If I can't do it every day, I'm not a real athlete," Harpreet said.
On the fourth morning Sukhi was at the door at dawn with both their shoes. "Just to the peepal tree. Not the canal." Harpreet grumbled, then laced up.

qa.q: Why did Harpreet sleep through the morning run?
qa.a: Her cousin's wedding kept the whole house awake till three.

qa.q: Why did Harpreet feel she had 'ruined it' after one missed run?
qa.a: Harpreet felt crushed and disappointed, believing a real athlete never misses a day, so one miss seemed proof that all five weeks were wasted.

qa.q: What choice of Sukhi's could break the all-or-nothing pattern?
qa.a: Turning up at dawn with both pairs of shoes and suggesting a shorter run to the peepal tree, making the restart small and easy.

qa.q: How might Sukhi see Harpreet's decision to quit?
qa.a: As an overreaction, since from outside one missed day barely counts next to five weeks of running.

grounding: A village teenager training for athletics misses one morning run and decides the whole plan is ruined, until her cousin suggests a small restart.

subtype: Skipping practice after a bad day [Actor]
passage:
Emeka had a chart on his bedroom wall in Lagos: forty press-ups and a jog around the estate every day before school, forty days in a row, to get fit for the football season. He had ticked off seventeen days. On day eighteen a thunderstorm flooded the road, and he stayed in.
That evening he tore the chart down. "Plan's dead," he told his friend Wei on the phone. "I broke it."
"Because of rain?" Wei asked.
"It doesn't count unless it's every single day," Emeka said. "Otherwise it's just... nothing."
He didn't do press-ups the next day either, or the next. On Saturday Wei turned up with a new chart drawn in marker, with a column for "rain days" already on it. "Seventeen plus today," Wei said. "Go."

qa.q: How many days had Emeka ticked off before the storm?
qa.a: Seventeen days.

qa.q: Why did Emeka tear the chart down after one rainy day?
qa.a: In his thinking only a perfect streak counts, so one missed day turned the whole plan into 'nothing'.

qa.q: Why might Wei's new chart with a 'rain days' column help?
qa.a: It builds in room for misses and still counts the seventeen days, giving Emeka a middle ground between perfect and pointless. 👍

qa.q: What might Wei have felt hearing 'Plan's dead' over rain?
qa.a: Surprised and a bit worried to see a friend throw away real progress, which is why Wei came round with a new chart.

grounding: A teenager in Nigeria misses one day of a forty-day fitness plan because of a storm and declares the whole plan dead.

passage:
At the district swimming club in Nagpur, Yogesh, fourteen, had a laminated card clipped to his kit bag: Mon, Wed, Fri, Sat, 5:30 a.m., every week till the state trials.

For six weeks he didn't miss once. Then on Wednesday his grandfather was unwell and the family spent the night at the hospital. Yogesh slept through his alarm on Thursday and missed Friday too, just from tiredness.

On Saturday, his friend Dhruv found him sitting on the bench outside the pool, still in school clothes.

"You're not changing?"

"What's the point? The card's broken. Two misses. Either you do the plan or you don't."

"You did twenty-four sessions."

"And missed two. So it doesn't count." Yogesh unclipped the card and dropped it in the bin by the gate. He walked out before the whistle blew.

qa.q: Where did Yogesh drop the card?
qa.a: He dropped it in the bin by the gate.

qa.q: Why does "Either you do the plan or you don't" feel reasonable to Yogesh?
qa.a: For six weeks the plan was perfect, and being perfect was what made it feel real. With two misses, Yogesh can only see it as broken, so quitting feels logical rather than giving up.

qa.q: What could Dhruv or the coach suggest to Yogesh at this turning point?
qa.a: Treat the missed days as a gap, not an ending, and just swim Saturday's session. A rule like "get back in at the next session" gives a middle option between perfect and pointless.

qa.q: How might Dhruv feel watching Yogesh walk out before the whistle?
qa.a: Dhruv may feel frustrated or sad, having seen Yogesh train hard for six weeks. It could also be hard to know what to say to a friend who won't listen.

grounding: A teenage swimmer who misses sessions after a family emergency decides the whole plan is over, seeing only perfect or pointless.

passage:
Subject: the yoga plan

Hi Afreen Apa,

Thanks again for making me that 30-day yoga and stretching plan. I know you spent a whole evening on the chart.

I'm writing to say I'm stopping. I did the first 11 days, every single morning, even on Sunday. Then on Monday I had a maths test and I stayed up late revising, and I just didn't do it in the morning. So the 30 days are broken.

I know you'll say "just carry on", but it isn't really 30 days if there's a gap. It's 11 days and then 18 days, which is a different thing. I'd rather start properly in the summer holidays, when nothing can interrupt it.

Please don't be annoyed. My back does feel better, by the way. Weird.

Zubin

P.S. I've taken the chart off my wall so I don't have to look at the empty box.

qa.q: How many days of the plan did Zubin complete before stopping?
qa.a: Zubin did the first 11 days.

qa.q: Why does Zubin want to wait for the summer holidays?
qa.a: Zubin feels discouraged that the 30 days are "broken" and believes a plan only counts if it's unbroken, so starting again when nothing can interrupt it feels like the only proper way.

qa.q: What would you advise Zubin to do tomorrow morning?
qa.a: Do Day 12 anyway and cross out the empty box without drama. Noticing that Zubin's back already feels better is a reason to keep going, not to restart in summer.

qa.q: How might Afreen Apa feel reading this email?
qa.a: Afreen might be a bit sad that the chart Afreen spent an evening on is off the wall, but also see that Zubin is being too harsh with a single missed morning. Afreen could reply by pointing out that eleven days already helped Zubin's back.

grounding: A teenager emails Afreen Apa that one missed morning means the whole exercise plan is broken, seeing only a perfect streak or nothing.
